video.title: The Most Overlooked $13K/Day Business Anyone Can Start

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Hunter about starting a parking-lot maintenance business with line striping, then adding seal coating and crack filling. Hunter describes learning with a small free job, finding customers through local Facebook posts and email, and growing from small striping jobs to larger contracts. He shares pricing, equipment costs, job economics, and the physical work involved. The main takeaway is that low-cost striping can open the door to higher-value maintenance work, but delivery still requires people, equipment, and attention to weather and job conditions.

speakers.name: Hunter
speakers.description: Parking-lot striping and asphalt maintenance operator; surname not stated.

ideas.name: Parking-lot line striping
ideas.one_liner: Repaint parking lines, symbols, and directional markings for churches and other businesses.
ideas.business_model: Per-line and per-stencil job pricing, with a minimum charge; striping can lead to seal-coating and crack-filling work.
ideas.customer: Churches and other businesses with parking lots that need new or refreshed lines and markings.
ideas.problem: Faded, missing, or poorly aligned parking lines and markings make a lot look neglected and can make it harder to use.
ideas.offer: Repaint parking stalls, handicapped symbols, arrows, fire lanes, and no-parking areas. Hunter sometimes covers poor old markings and gives a small number of blue handicapped symbols as a free extra.

pricing.model: Per line, per stencil or marked area, with a minimum job price.
pricing.notes: Hunter said travel and hard-to-see lines that need to be realigned can raise his per-line price. He said he quotes some stencils at $10 or $25. The transcript also includes a $760 quote for a particular church lot and estimates for materials and labor.

acquisition_channels.details: Hunter bought scraped prospect lists from a contractor on Upwork and emailed churches and businesses. His message said he was new, would offer a good price, and wanted to make the church look good for Christmas. He said he sent about 50 emails on his first day and around 300 total in an early campaign.

quote.text: So email I I work with a guy overseas just on Upwork found him and I pay him five or six bucks for a list that he provides.
quote.speaker: Hunter

acquisition_channels.details: He posted in his town's Facebook page asking people to vote for a business that should get a new lot. He used the free job to get his name in front of local business owners and then contacted nominated businesses about paid work.

quote.text: So, I went on Facebook, made a post in our town's page, and just said, "Hey, I'd love to help out a business. Vote below for for who you want to see have a new lot."
quote.speaker: Hunter

acquisition_channels.details: He tried door knocking but found it was not the best use of his time. He also preferred to meet prospects in person to quote jobs when possible; he said his close rate was better in person.

quote.text: So, I I did go door knocking. That was hard. It didn't feel like it was the best use of my time, so I yeah, jumped into email.
quote.speaker: Hunter

ideas.delivery: Hunter practices on an old lot with water, then does a small free nonprofit job before taking paid work. He visits sites to quote when possible, measures and prices the lines and stencils, and applies water-based paint with a striping machine. A roller and paint can be used when machine access is unavailable, but require more taping and time. Hunter said he sometimes hires help when work exceeds his capacity.
unit_economics_claims: Hunter said he spent $5 on paint for his first small free job.
He quoted one church $1,190, later completed a similar church job for around $1,000 to $1,200, and said his first month brought just over $2,800.
Hunter said first-month profit was about 75% because he did the work himself.
A particular church lot with 82 parking stalls was quoted at $760; Hunter estimated about $130 in materials and Chris estimated about $200 in total costs and $550 in profit.
Hunter said his minimum job price had risen to $500.
tools: Graco line striping machine, models 3400 and 3900
ideas.startup_cost: Hunter said he started the business with just over $3,000. He described a lower-cost roller-and-paint route, but the transcript gives different figures: Chris mentioned a $10 roller, while Hunter later said rollers cost $20. Hunter bought a used striping machine for $2,300 and a stencil pack for $800.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. Hunter first practiced with water, did a small nonprofit lot for free, then obtained paid work through email.

acquisition.how: Lead-list preparation and email drafting could be assisted by software, but targeting, replies, site visits, and in-person sales require human judgment. In-person selling caps practical automation.

onboarding.how: A form could collect site details, but someone still needs to inspect the lot, assess faded lines and stencils, and confirm the quote.

delivery.how: People must prepare the site and physically paint the lines and markings.

billing.how: Quote IQ can prepare quotes; routine invoicing could be automated, though Hunter said many church customers pay by check.

support.how: Agents could answer routine scheduling and quote questions, but complaints and site-specific changes need a person.

uk_applicability.notes: The service transfers to UK car parks, but markings, accessible-bay requirements, insurance, and site-safety practices need to fit UK rules and customer expectations. UK cold-email rules allow unsolicited marketing to corporate subscribers, but not to individuals or sole traders without consent; prospect lists must be screened accordingly.

risks: Door knocking was a poor use of Hunter's time.
Church board approval took a couple of weeks, delaying paid work.
A used machine required replacement parts and learning how to repair it.
Hunter said he spilled two gallons of paint in his minivan.
Faded or misaligned lines can take longer and cost more to fix than a simple repaint.
Work is weather-sensitive; Hunter described a rush to finish before it got too cold.
Unsolicited UK marketing email must follow PECR; avoid sending to individuals or sole traders without consent.

ideas.name: Parking-lot seal coating
ideas.one_liner: Apply a protective asphalt coating to extend the life and improve the appearance of parking lots.
ideas.business_model: Per-square-foot job pricing, with larger projects often sold alongside striping.
ideas.customer: Churches and other owners or operators of asphalt parking lots.
ideas.problem: Asphalt deteriorates and looks worn; sealing is intended to protect the pavement and make it look better.
ideas.offer: Spray a thin layer of asphalt seal coating over a prepared parking lot. Hunter added this service after customers asking for striping also requested seal-coating quotes.

pricing.notes: The $9,000-plus lot quote is an example, not a universal price. The speakers discussed labor and profit estimates for that example.

acquisition_channels.details: Hunter said customers who first wanted striping also asked for seal-coating quotes. He added the service because he found that subcontractors were busy or unsuitable.

quote.text: I started when I would go meet these these people to give them quotes. I I would try to always go in person and they always wanted striping and sealing.
quote.speaker: Hunter

acquisition_channels.details: Hunter's email outreach targeted churches and businesses for parking-lot work, which created opportunities to quote sealing as well as striping.

quote.text: So email I I work with a guy overseas just on Upwork found him and I pay him five or six bucks for a list that he provides.
quote.speaker: Hunter

ideas.delivery: Hunter tows a 275-gallon tank and spray system behind a truck and sprays the asphalt surface. The work takes a full day for the example lot. He said he uses two workers for some jobs and charges 50% upfront because material costs are higher. Freshly sealed pavement may require more careful striping and chalk-line layout afterward.
unit_economics_claims: Hunter quoted just over $9,000 to seal a 46,900-square-foot lot.
He said material cost was about $0.06 per square foot and his selling price was usually $0.15 to $0.25 per square foot.
For the example lot, Chris estimated around $3,000 in material, two workers at $300 each, and about $4,500 profit; Hunter agreed the job could have about a 50% net margin after overhead.
Hunter said his best one-day seal-coating job brought in $13,000; striping the same site was done the next day for $1,700.
He said a large church job was worth $26,000.
ideas.startup_cost: Hunter bought a used seal-coating trailer with a tank and pump for $6,000. He did not state the total cost of starting this service.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. Hunter took a seal-coating job after customers began requesting quotes; he said he drove three hours to collect equipment for an early job.

acquisition.how: Existing striping customers can be identified in a CRM, but site visits, quoting, and relationship-based sales remain human work.

onboarding.how: Satellite measurements can help estimate area, but site condition, preparation, access, and scope need human review.

delivery.how: Workers must tow equipment, prepare the site, spray the coating, and manage the physical job.

billing.how: Invoices and 50% deposit requests can be automated, but payment timing and job completion need human oversight.

support.how: Automated scheduling and routine updates are feasible; site problems and customer decisions need a person.

uk_applicability.notes: Commercial asphalt lots exist in the UK, but material specifications, local climate, waste handling, site safety, and customer expectations need local adaptation. Weather affects when work can be done. UK cold-email rules apply to prospecting.

risks: Hunter said subcontractors could not take the work soon enough or were poor-quality options, so offering the service may require buying equipment and learning the work.
Weather can compress the working season and create long, demanding days.
Material costs are high enough that Hunter takes 50% upfront.
Faint lines after sealing may need to be measured or re-laid with a chalk line.
Oil-based striping paint on a seal-coated surface can turn yellow and hazy, according to Hunter.
The example profit calculations were estimates and did not fully itemize insurance, gas, and overhead.

ideas.name: Parking-lot crack filling
ideas.one_liner: Fill asphalt cracks to slow deterioration and reduce the chance of larger cracks and potholes.
ideas.business_model: Per-linear-foot pricing or an estimated project price for lots with many cracks.
ideas.customer: Churches and other owners or operators of asphalt parking lots.
ideas.problem: Cracks can widen and develop into potholes, shortening the useful life and harming the appearance of a parking lot.
ideas.offer: Measure and fill asphalt cracks with heated material. Hunter said he sometimes estimates rather than measuring every crack in a complex lot.

pricing.model: Usually priced per linear foot, with total job prices depending on the number and depth of cracks.
pricing.notes: Hunter corrected himself from square-foot to linear-foot pricing. He said material use varies substantially with crack depth.

acquisition_channels.details: Crack filling was added after customers who asked for striping and sealing also requested quotes for it.

quote.text: So, I started with striping and then everyone wanted those quotes for seal coating and crack filling.
quote.speaker: Hunter

acquisition_channels.details: The same church and business email outreach used for striping could lead to quotes for crack filling.

quote.text: So email I I work with a guy overseas just on Upwork found him and I pay him five or six bucks for a list that he provides.
quote.speaker: Hunter

ideas.delivery: Hunter pushes a measuring wheel along cracks, heats material with propane using a crack-filling machine, then walks the crack and applies the material. Heating takes about 20 minutes, while the example 38-foot crack took about two minutes to fill. The work is physical and material use varies with crack depth.
unit_economics_claims: Hunter said he charges $0.30 to $1 per linear foot.
He gave an example of a 38-foot crack priced at $38 and estimated $5 to $10 in material for that crack.
He said the smallest crack-filling job he had was over $400 and most jobs were $2,000 to $3,000.
Hunter said a badly misquoted job with cracks six or seven inches deep took two days and left him with no profit.
He estimated a safe gross margin of around 70%, while saying results depend on crack depth.
ideas.startup_cost: Hunter bought a new crack-filling machine for $1,500. He did not state total startup cost for this service.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. Hunter said he bought equipment after landing his first crack-filling job.

acquisition.how: Existing customer records and automated email workflows can identify prospects, but quotes and site assessment remain human-led.

onboarding.how: A customer can submit site details online, but someone must inspect crack depth and estimate material needs.

delivery.how: Workers must heat material and physically apply it along the cracks.

billing.how: A quoting and invoicing system can automate routine billing, though the scope and final amount may change after inspection.

support.how: Agents could handle scheduling and routine questions, but variation in site conditions requires human support.

uk_applicability.notes: The service is relevant to UK asphalt car parks, but materials, safety procedures, local climate, and disposal requirements need to be checked against UK practice. UK cold-email rules apply to prospecting.

risks: Crack depth can be difficult to judge from appearance and can consume far more material than expected.
Hunter described working two days on a badly quoted job and making nothing.
Heating material and applying it are physical, equipment-dependent tasks.
Very small isolated cracks may not justify mobilization; Hunter said his smallest job exceeded $400.
UK customer outreach must follow PECR rules.

tactics.name: Practice before taking a paid job
steps: Find an old parking lot and practice following existing lines with water in the machine.
Do a very small free job for a nonprofit to learn how the work feels and build confidence.
Track material use and adjust technique before quoting larger sites.

warnings.warning: Hunter said a crack-filling job with cracks six or seven inches deep consumed enough material that he worked for two days and walked away with no profit.
Used striping equipment was cheaper but required Hunter to replace some parts and learn repairs.
Church customers may need board approval, which Hunter said can take a couple of weeks.
Seal coating and striping work is exposed to weather; Hunter described rushing to complete jobs before colder conditions arrived.
For asphalt Hunter recommended water-based paint; he said oil-based paint on a seal-coated surface can turn yellow and hazy.
Hunter said he initially tried door knocking but found it was not the best use of his time.
The host's sponsor segment makes claims about LLC liability protection and tax write-offs; those are promotional claims, not independently established in the interview.
The host promoted a paid business community, and Hunter promoted online guides and in-person training, creating promotional conflicts around business advice.

For UK outreach, do not copy the US-style email tactic without checking PECR: unsolicited marketing email to individuals and sole traders generally requires consent, while corporate subscribers may be contacted subject to applicable rules.
